notes.meaning: Jesus asks the crowd what they expected to find when they went into the desert to hear John. John was indeed a true prophet carrying God's word, but his calling was even greater than that of earlier prophets because he pointed directly to the Messiah.
Jesus explains that the prophet Malachi had written about John hundreds of years earlier. John was God's royal messenger sent ahead of the Lord to prepare people's hearts to receive him.

Jesus praises John as the greatest person born under the old covenant because of his unique role. Yet anyone who enters the kingdom of God under the new covenant holds an even greater position, enjoying full forgiveness and the Holy Spirit living within them.

Ordinary people and even despised tax collectors agreed that God's way was right when they heard John preach. By accepting John's baptism, they admitted their sins and welcomed God's call to repentance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars observe that the ordinary people who accepted John's baptism are said to justify God, directly linking them to wisdom's children who vindicate God in verse 35.

notes.meaning: The religious leaders and legal experts thought they were already good enough and did not need to repent. By refusing John's baptism, they rejected God's gracious plan for their lives and harmed their own souls.

Jesus compares the stubborn leaders to children playing games in the market who refuse to join in. When one group played happy flute tunes for a wedding game, the others would not dance; when they sang sad funeral songs, the others would not weep. Nothing pleased them.

John lived an austere life in the wilderness, fasting and drinking no wine, to call people to serious repentance. Instead of taking his warning to heart, his critics dismissed him and claimed he was demon-possessed.

Jesus came sharing normal meals and spending time with social outcasts in order to save them. Rather than seeing his mercy, his critics slandered him as a glutton, a drunkard, and a friend of bad company.
God's true wisdom is proved right by the lives of those who follow it. The repentant people who responded to John and Jesus showed that God's different ways of reaching them were good and right.

A Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to his home for a meal, and Jesus accepted. At such formal meals, guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow with their feet stretched out behind them.

A local woman known for leading an immoral life learned where Jesus was eating. She bravely entered the house carrying an expensive jar made of smooth alabaster stone, filled with sweet-smelling perfume.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A long-held popular tradition claims this woman was Mary Magdalene, though the Gospels introduce Mary Magdalene as a different person in the very next chapter.

notes.meaning: Standing behind Jesus at his feet, the woman was overcome with sorrow for her sins and gratitude for his mercy. Her tears fell like rain onto his feet, and she let down her hair to wipe them dry before repeatedly kissing his feet and pouring perfume on them.
Simon watched her and concluded that Jesus could not be a prophet. He assumed that a true man of God would know how sinful she was and would never allow an unclean person to touch him.
Jesus proved he truly was a prophet by answering the quiet thoughts Simon had kept to himself. He spoke gently to his host, and Simon invited him to share what was on his mind.

Jesus told a short story about a moneylender who cancelled the debts of two men who were unable to pay him back. One owed five hundred silver coins, worth almost two years of labor, while the other owed fifty. Jesus then asked Simon which debtor would love the moneylender more.
Simon replied that the person who had the larger debt cancelled would surely feel the greatest love. Jesus told him that his answer was entirely correct.

Jesus turned toward the woman and contrasted her devotion with Simon's coldness. Simon had failed to offer ordinary courtesies to his guest: he gave no water for dusty feet, no friendly kiss of greeting, and no oil for Jesus' head. In contrast, the woman washed his feet with tears, kissed them constantly, and anointed them with costly perfume.

The woman's deep love did not earn her pardon; rather, her outpouring of affection was the clear proof that her many sins had already been forgiven. A person who thinks they need little forgiveness will show only little love.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic interpretation understands the verse to mean that her great love was the ground or reason her sins were forgiven, rather than only the evidence of it.

notes.meaning: Jesus spoke directly to the woman and announced that her sins were forgiven. His spoken words gave her public assurance and deep comfort, quieting any fear of judgment.
The other dinner guests were startled and began questioning among themselves who Jesus thought he was. They knew that God alone has the power and right to wipe away human sin.
Jesus told the woman that her faith in him had saved her, not the good deeds she had performed. He sent her away with a promise of peace, assuring her that she was fully reconciled to God.
